output_text: {"assessment_summary":"The manuscript effectively addresses the significant challenge of improving healthcare in low-income countries, specifically through the governance of non-profit health centers in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The randomized program provides a robust experimental design, comparing health centers receiving performance-based funding bundled with auditing and feedback (A&F) to those receiving funding alone. The empirical results indicate that the governance treatment significantly enhances both operating efficiency and health outcomes, an important finding considering the literature often critiques the effectiveness of performance-based funding in these contexts. Furthermore, the authors elucidate mechanisms through qualitative insights from interviews, reinforcing the link between governance structures and improved service delivery. However, while the study is strong, it does discuss some limitations, notably the specificity of its findings to the healthcare sector and their generalizability. The analysis also lacks exploration of potential confounding variables beyond the treatment and control groups. Future research could benefit from examining whether these governance mechanisms apply to other non-profit sectors in various contexts, and dissecting the individual contributions of each governance element (performance-based funding vs. A&F).
